B_access_pricing.mcp_access_cost_details: No separate MCP fee is stated. Sanity says the remote server is available to all Sanity projects; a Sanity account and authorization are required.
B_access_pricing.linked_software_cost: Free: $0/month; Growth: $15 per seat/month; Enterprise: custom pricing.
B_access_pricing.pricing_model_details: Sanity's pricing page describes monthly project plans and per-seat Growth billing. The MCP documentation says generate_image and transform_image consume AI credits; most other MCP tools do not. Credit costs vary by action.
B_access_pricing.other_access_restrictions: OAuth is the default. A bearer API token can be configured instead, and calls then use that token's role and permissions. Manually configured OAuth sessions typically expire after seven days. No MCP-specific paid tier or per-call price was found.
B_access_pricing.restrictions_controlled_by: Vendor and Sanity project/organization permission configuration

C_capabilities.description_what_how: The official documentation lists 54 tools for content, schemas, releases, projects, datasets, media libraries, documentation, development rules, and feedback. Their availability at the input endpoint is supported by its authentication challenge and official endpoint documentation.

The materials reviewed do not specify MCP-call logging, audit event format, or an MCP logging capability. General Sanity plan features include audit history and request logs, but their connection to MCP calls is not stated.

The endpoint returns an OAuth bearer challenge. Supplied protected-resource metadata names https://mcp.sanity.io as the authorization server, declares scopes_supported ["global"] and bearer_methods_supported ["header"]. Authorization-server metadata declares authorization_code and refresh_token grants, S256 PKCE, token endpoint authentication methods client_secret_basic, client_secret_post, and none, plus a registration endpoint. OpenID configuration returned 404. Docs also describe bearer API-token authentication.
C_capabilities.pre_interaction_context_verbatim: WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token", error_description="Missing Authorization header", resource_metadata="https://mcp.sanity.io/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp"
C_capabilities.post_interaction_context_structure: The endpoint's unauthenticated response is JSON: {"error":"invalid_token","error_description":"Missing Authorization header"}. Token response format and token lifetime are not specified in the supplied metadata; docs say manually configured OAuth sessions typically expire after seven days.
C_capabilities.authorization_mechanism: OAuth protected-resource metadata and Dynamic Client Registration are advertised. Authorization Code and Refresh Token grants; PKCE S256; token auth methods client_secret_basic, client_secret_post, none; scopes_supported: global. Revocation endpoint https://mcp.sanity.io/revoke; registration endpoint https://mcp.sanity.io/register. Docs additionally permit a bearer API token whose role and permissions govern tool calls.

D_server_side_logic.additional_logic: 1. The official list includes reads, writes, and destructive operations. The hosted docs do not publish tool annotations such as readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, or openWorldHint. 2. No server-enforced general confirmation flow is documented. Docs recommend draft/release workflows and describe writes that take effect immediately, including cdnAccessPolicy edits. 3. OAuth scope metadata advertises only global; docs say calls follow the user's Sanity role or API-token permissions. OAuth sessions typically expire after seven days. 4. No read-only endpoint, URL tool filter, or MCP sandbox mode is documented. Writes often stage as drafts or release versions; release scheduling and deletion are outside the documented MCP tools. 5. Media Library patching is limited to documented fields and schema validation; no general PII masking or secret-redaction policy is documented. 6. Asset status checks accept 1–20 operation IDs; dataset document patching is capped at 25 documents per call; dataset file uploads are capped at 50 MiB; query results larger than 64 KiB are rejected. Upload docs mention source size and fetch-time limits, without numeric values. AI image generation and transformation consume AI credits. 7. Media Library writes are schema-validated; invalid edits and certain system fields are rejected. Docs do not specify unknown-argument handling or operator overrides. 8. Sanity plan pages advertise audit history and request logs, but MCP-specific logging behavior is not stated. 9. give_sanity_feedback asks agents to submit issue/workflow feedback to Sanity. No separate rating or survey tool is listed; AI-credit charges and upgrade links are documented in product pricing/error guidance. 10. get_sanity_rules/list_sanity_rules expose development rules through tools. Tool descriptions also instruct agents on sequencing, batching, and retry checks; whether those recommendations are enforced is tool-specific. 11. No agent-history-dependent behavior is documented. 12. This endpoint's documented tool list is flat; separate Sanity Context MCP is a distinct server. Asset operations use asynchronous operation IDs. 13. run_sanity_cli is a restricted command interface, not a raw shell: docs say it cannot access files, prompt, run in the background, or change authentication. query_documents accepts GROQ, while CLI/API calls are not described as arbitrary raw HTTP access.
behavioural_instructions_to_ai_verbatim: Check the destination before repeating an upload whose outcome is unknown.
Honor HTTP Retry-After when rate limited.
Use `list_workspace_schemas` when several schema sources are available, then pass the advertised `schemaId` to inspect that exact schema.
Do not patch the published or draft ID first because that creates an unrelated draft.
For unfamiliar GROQ syntax, functions, or query patterns, fetch get_sanity_rules({rules: ["groq"]}) before proceeding.

E_aggregated.token_method: No deployed-server code or verbatim complete tools/list and initialize payload was available; documentation lists names and descriptions, not full definitions and schemas.
E_aggregated.human_can_agent_cannot: The documented MCP tools do not schedule, publish, archive, or delete a content release; Sanity says these must be done in Studio or via the HTTP Actions API. The Media Library MCP tools do not support folder placement or version-graph management; docs direct users to the Media Library app. The server's CLI tool cannot change authentication or access the filesystem. Sources: https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/mcp-server

F_documentation.implementation_hints_not_enforced: Tool descriptions recommend checking destinations before upload retries, honoring Retry-After, batching status checks, creating release versions before patching, and loading GROQ rules for unfamiliar syntax. These instructions are provided in tool descriptions; the documentation does not state that every recommendation is enforced by the server.
F_documentation.governance_promises: Sanity says calls use the authenticated user's role or token permissions. The Terms say Subscriber Data may be processed as needed to provide the Service and that Service Usage Data may be used for Sanity's business purposes. The reviewed MCP docs do not make MCP-specific retention, AI-training, or audit-logging promises.
F_documentation.promises_to_user: Sanity describes the remote server as hosted on its infrastructure, OAuth-enabled, continuously updated, and available without a local install. Its MCP page says edits respect the deployed schema and that most MCP tools do not consume AI credits.
F_documentation.comparison_with_server_logic: Permission inheritance is described for bearer-token calls. Media Library schema checks and field restrictions are documented as enforced behaviors. OAuth session expiry and rate-limit guidance are documented; the latter is advice to clients. Hosted, continuously updated operation is a product claim, not a tool-level governance mechanism. General audit logs are listed as plan features, with no MCP-specific linkage stated.

contradictions: The official tool reference documents 54 tools, while the Claude connector directory reports 31 and exposes 23 names in the captured page. The directory's five additional visible names—create_documents_from_json, create_documents_from_markdown, migration_guide, patch_document_from_json, and patch_document_from_markdown—are not in the official list; they are retained as third-party-only entries.

The OAuth protected-resource documents advertise scopes_supported ["global"], while product documentation says calls use the user's role/token permissions. The materials do not explain how the global OAuth scope maps to Sanity product roles.
observations_for_research: The official tool descriptions include operational sequencing and retry guidance that can influence agent call patterns even where general confirmation is not documented.
Several write tools use drafts or release versions, while some Media Library fields take effect immediately; this yields different staging behavior within the same server.
The docs describe two AI-credit-consuming tools and separately describe server calls that generally do not consume credits.
notes: Checked the provided links.json, pages/ text, script text and HTML, links_check.txt, and the public GitHub repository page. The official repository is an archived deprecated local server, not code for the hosted endpoint; the repository was not present in the local code folder, and its commit and implementation details were not used. The official docs page publishes tool names and descriptions but not complete schemas or hosted initialize instructions. The supplied OAuth metadata was used without re-fetching. Unofficial/proxy listings were excluded from actions; OpenMCP's listing is a separate proxy. Pricing and legal findings reflect the captured official pages.
